cues.text: Jane, what did you think of Professor Morgan’s lecture?
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: I don’t know about you, but I find it incredibly difficult to believe that light influences the environment as much as he says.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: I’ve never seen any journal articles, websites or anything that verifies his argument. It’s stupid.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: On the contrary, I’ve seen a great deal of research supporting his argument from a wide range of renowned scientists.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: Have you looked at the recommended textbook listed on the course outline given to us at the beginning of the semester?
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: All the information is in there, perhaps you’ve just been looking in the wrong places.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: I never look at the course outlines, I have so many loose sheets of paper I tend to lose anything I’m given by the end of the day.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: What’s the textbook they recommend, and where can I get it from?
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: I should probably go buy it soon; I’m already behind in the course.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Yeah, you definitely should buy it, and our grades are more important this year!
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: It’s called ‘The Influence of Light on the Environment’. You should be able to find it in the bookshop on campus.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: If not, they’ll order it within two weeks.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: In the meantime, you should read up on Ken Simpson’s work, he argues that in order to protect natural habitats, governments should endeavor to turn off lights in cities at night.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: Well that’s controversial; I doubt any government would be willing to do that any time soon.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: I imagine roads would become quite dangerous without street lighting.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: For this issue, Dave Kepler suggests they could just replace the existing lights with more environmentally friendly bulbs.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: They could even install solar-powered lights; that way, roads will be more eco-friendly while maintaining safety.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Although I guess they wouldn’t be particularly effective in colder countries, especially during the winter.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: That’s quite a good idea actually.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: The price of solar power is supposed to be on par with electricity within the next few decades, and it was on the news this morning.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: I’ve also heard that, according to Sharon Grey, in countries with more sunlight, insect-eating animals tend to be smaller in size.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: Since there are fewer insects, and the remaining insects produced a smaller number of eggs.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: Yeah, I think I read somewhere that sunlight also has a negative effect on the quality of water, but I’m not sure I believe it.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: In many hot countries, particularly developing countries, there is a lot of water pollution caused by factories rather than sunlight.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Nevertheless, Maria Jackson says that in direct sunlight, the surface of the water becomes more translucent, therefore it affects the amount of sunlight that aquatic insects can absorb.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Not much research has been undertaken to prove Jackson’s theory, but it seems to have been widely accepted anyway.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: I’ve never heard of that. I’ll have to look it up on Google.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: The only other theory I’ve studied is Barbara Swallow’s study on how declined insect population adversely affects the frog population.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: Not that I’m complaining.. .I hate insects, especially spiders.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: You have arachnophobia? I never would have guessed.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Didn’t your brother have a pet black widow spider?
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Yes, he did, and I hated it. It escaped from its cage once and we never found it.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: I had nightmares for months.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: Okay, now I’m getting goose bumps, let’s change the subject.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: What’s your stance on natural and artificial light?
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: Honestly, I’m not sure it makes much difference which one you use; species will die out either way.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: I think the real argument we should consider is global warming and protection or replacement of finite fuels.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Solar power provides us with an incredible opportunity to replace electricity, and governments should definitely increase spending on research in this field.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: The theories discussed in our lectures, like Simpson’s and Grey’s, are so vague and lack proof, so I don’t understand why we even study them.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: I see what you mean. I don’t like learning unsupported theories for exams, and I’d rather spend my time learning something else.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: For example, I’d be much more interested in studying the animals in safari parks than researching migratory birds, particularly the effect of tourists on the quality of life of animals.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: As we know, every year thousands of visitors will drive in their own vehicles or ride in vehicles provided by the facility to observe freely roaming animals.
cues.speaker: Jane

cues.text: Yeah, that would be really interesting!
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Especially those animals living in more tropical countries, like Borneo.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Following on from that, I want to study how bringing animals over from foreign countries to put in our zoos affects their life expectancy.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: For example, do you remember when China sent pandas to Edinburgh Zoo?
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: Apparently one of the pandas became depressed, but it was never explained why.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: To me, obviously, you can’t take an animal out of its natural habitat and put it in a cage on the other side of the world.
cues.speaker: Jim

cues.text: It just doesn’t work...
cues.speaker: Jim
